title: Thessalonica, Berea, and Paul at Athens
summary: Paul reasons in the synagogue at Thessalonica that the Christ had to suffer and rise, and many believe, but a mob accuses the believers of defying Caesar by proclaiming another king. At Berea the hearers examine the Scriptures daily, until opponents arrive from Thessalonica. At Athens, troubled by the city's idols, Paul debates in the marketplace and addresses the council of the Areopagus about the unknown God, the Creator who now commands all people to repent and has raised a man from the dead as the world's judge.
story: Having crossed into Macedonia, Paul moves west along the main road from city to city, and each stop is shorter than the last as opposition follows him. The chapter then brings him to Athens, the symbolic heart of Greek culture and philosophy, and Luke gives us Paul's best-known speech to Gentiles. The Lystra speech in chapter 14 was a quick protest to a crowd; this is a considered address to the educated elite. Together with the synagogue sermon in chapter 13 and the farewell to church leaders in chapter 20, it shows Paul speaking to each of his main audiences. After Athens he will go on to Corinth, where he stays much longer.
historical:
Amphipolis and Apollonia were stages on the Via Egnatia, the Roman road that ran west through Macedonia. Thessalonica (modern Thessaloniki) was the capital of the province of Macedonia and a free city, which allowed it to govern its own affairs. Luke calls its officials politarchs, city rulers. That title was once thought unusual, but it has since been found in a number of inscriptions from Thessalonica and other Macedonian towns, and it confirms the accuracy of Luke's detail. Paul's First Letter to the Thessalonians, written soon afterward, probably from Corinth around AD 50 or 51, reflects the same situation: a young church that received the word in much affliction and turned to God from idols (1 Thessalonians 1:6, 9).

Athens in Paul's day had long since lost its political power, but it remained a place of learning and prestige, still honored for its schools of philosophy. The Areopagus, the hill of Ares, gave its name to the city's ancient council, which in the Roman period still had authority over religious and educational matters. Scholars differ on whether Paul spoke on the hill itself or before the council meeting elsewhere, perhaps in the marketplace; the phrase in verse 22 can be read as the meeting of the Areopagus, the council. Either way, this was an inquiry, not necessarily a trial.
cultural:
The Epicureans followed Epicurus (died about 270 BC), who taught that the gods, if they exist, are remote and uninvolved, that the soul dissolves at death, and that the good life is a calm free from fear and pain. The Stoics followed Zeno of Citium (around 300 BC), who taught that divine reason pervades everything and that the wise person lives in harmony with nature. Both would have found bodily resurrection strange. The word translated babbler is spermologos, a seed-picker, used of birds and of people who pick up scraps of ideas and pass them off as learning.

Ancient writers such as the travel writer Pausanias mention altars at Athens dedicated to unknown gods, set up so that no deity would be neglected. Paul takes one as his starting point. The line We are His offspring comes from the Phaenomena of Aratus, a third-century BC poet from Cilicia, Paul's own region; a similar phrase appears in a hymn by the Stoic Cleanthes. The line In Him we live and move and have our being is often attributed to the Cretan poet Epimenides, though the attribution is less secure. At Thessalonica, the charge that the believers proclaim another king touched a raw nerve, since cities in the eastern empire swore loyalty oaths to the emperor.
literary: The chapter has three scenes of decreasing length for the Macedonian cities and increasing length for Athens. The Athens speech (verses 22-31) is carefully built. It opens with a courteous observation (you are very religious), takes the altar to an unknown God as its text, and then moves through a series of claims about God: he made the world, does not live in temples, needs nothing, gives life to all, made every nation from one man, and set their times and boundaries so that they would seek him. It quotes Greek poets rather than the Old Testament, but every claim is biblical at heart. It ends by turning from creation to judgment: God now commands repentance and has fixed a day of judgment, proven by the resurrection. At that point the speech is interrupted, as several speeches in Acts are.

outline.t: Reasoning from the Scriptures at Thessalonica
Uproar and the charge of another king
Paul in the marketplace at Athens
Mockery, interest, and a few believers

doctrines.note: Paul begins with the God who made the world and everything in it, who does not need anything from human beings but gives everyone life and breath. Creation is the foundation of his case against idols: a maker cannot be contained in something made.

Paul is deeply disturbed by a city full of idols, and he argues that since we are God's offspring, the Divine Being cannot be like gold or silver or stone. Idolatry is not only a mistake about God but a diminishing of the humans who bear his likeness.
God has set a day when He will judge the world with justice by the Man He has appointed. The resurrection of Jesus is presented as God's public proof that history is heading toward a just verdict.
The Bereans examined the Scriptures every day to test what they heard. The chapter commends hearers who weigh even an apostle's teaching against the written word.

words.note: Deisidaimon, religious. The word could mean devout in a good sense or superstitious in a bad one, fearful of spirits. Paul's opening line is ambiguous in a useful way: it is polite, but it also names the anxious multiplication of gods that his speech goes on to address.

Agnostos, unknown, the source of the English word agnostic. Paul turns the altar's admission into his opening: what you worship as something unknown, I now proclaim to you. The unknown God is the one who has made himself known.

Metanoeo, to repent, to change one's mind and direction. For Paul's Greek hearers, the call to repentance meant turning from idols to the living God and preparing for judgment. God, having overlooked earlier ignorance, now commands it of all people everywhere.

Anastasis, resurrection, literally a standing up again. Some Athenians seem to have thought Paul was proclaiming two new gods, Jesus and Anastasis. To Greek ears, the idea that a dead body would be raised was either absurd or unwelcome, which is why the speech is cut off at this word.

christ: At Thessalonica, Paul's message is that the Christ had to suffer and rise from the dead and that this Jesus is the Christ: Israel's Scriptures, rightly read, point to a suffering and risen Messiah. At Athens he never uses the word Christ, but his speech is still about Jesus. The appointed Man through whom God will judge the world is the one God raised from the dead. The Thessalonian mob grasped something true when it said the believers proclaimed another king named Jesus. The gospel was not a private spirituality that left the emperor's claims untouched; it declared that the risen Jesus is Lord of all, and every other ruler answers to him.

hard.q: Did Paul's approach at Athens fail, and did he regret it?
hard.a:
Some readers note that few believed at Athens, and that Paul later told the Corinthians he had resolved to know nothing among them except Jesus Christ and him crucified (1 Corinthians 2:2). They suggest that Paul learned from Athens that philosophical engagement was a mistake and changed his method at Corinth.

Others see no such regret. Luke presents the speech as a model, not a failure: some did believe, including a member of the council and a woman named Damaris, and the speech's content is consistent with Paul's letters (compare Romans 1:18-25). Paul's words to the Corinthians refer to the style and wisdom of rhetoric that Corinth prized, not to engaging with hearers' beliefs. On this view Athens shows that the gospel can begin where people are, with their questions and poets, without abandoning its center in the resurrection and judgment. Both readings agree that Paul did not tone down the resurrection, even when it provoked mockery.

questions: The Bereans tested Paul's teaching against Scripture every day. What would it look like to read the Bible that attentively?
Paul found a point of contact in an altar to an unknown God. What longings or questions in your culture might serve as a starting point for speaking about God?
Some Athenians mocked, some wanted to hear more, and some believed. Which of those responses is closest to your own reaction to the resurrection?
